title: Spark Liquidity Layer rate limits are deliberately asymmetric: inflows are capped and throttled while outflows are unlimited
content:
Every SparkLend Instance Configuration Document in this chunk pairs a bounded inflow with an unbounded outflow. The USDC instance (A.6.1.1.1.2.6.1.3.1.1.2.2.4.1/.2) sets inflow `maxAmount`: 100,000,000 USDC and `slope`: 200,000,000 USDC per day, and then states the outflow rate limits are "`maxAmount`: Unlimited" and "`slope`: Unlimited". Dai (.1.3.2.4), USDT (.1.4.2.4), pyUSD (.1.5.2.4) and wETH (.1.6.2.4) all repeat the same shape: a finite inflow, an `Unlimited` outflow `maxAmount`.

The asymmetry encodes a directional risk judgement. Sending Spark Liquidity Layer capital *into* an external lending venue creates new exposure, so it is throttled. Pulling capital *back* into the ALM Proxy reduces exposure, so throttling it would be actively harmful — a rate limit on withdrawal would become a hard ceiling on how fast the ecosystem can de-risk during a venue failure or depeg.

The trade-off is that the safety valve is one-directional by construction: the rate-limit machinery cannot be used to slow an exit even if a fast exit were itself destabilising (for example a withdrawal large enough to drain an external pool's liquidity and strand other lenders). Spark accepts that externality in exchange for guaranteeing its own escape velocity.

Read together with the per-instance keying of limits, this means the rate-limit system is best understood not as a risk *budget* but as an onboarding brake: it governs the speed at which new exposure can be built, and says nothing about the speed at which it is unwound.
description: Across every SparkLend instance the inflow leg carries both a maxAmount and a daily slope while the outflow leg is Unlimited, so recall of capital is never the binding constraint.
